title: Geographical indications
subtitle: Place as a legal promise
objectives: Explain what a geographical indication is
Explain why place names are protected

steps.title: What a GI is
steps.body: A geographical indication, or GI, is a legally defined area whose name can only be used by wines from there. Champagne, Rioja and Napa Valley are all GIs. Using the name promises origin, and often more: in Europe, rules may set grapes, yields and winemaking.
steps.highlight: A GI is a protected place name

steps.title: PDO and PGI
steps.body: The EU has two levels. PDO, Protected Designation of Origin, is stricter: grapes must all come from the area, and rules cover varieties, yields, methods and ageing. PGI, Protected Geographical Indication, covers larger areas with looser rules: at least 85% of grapes from the area, and wider grape choices. Each country has its own names for them.

steps.prompt: Match each term to its meaning.
steps.explanation: Each step down the ladder gives producers more freedom and the consumer less information about place.

steps.title: Why protection matters
steps.body: Place names became valuable, so others copied them. Before protection, sparkling wines worldwide called themselves Champagne. Today, EU agreements protect GIs in many countries. In the US, some older semi-generic names like California Champagne can still appear on bottles approved before 2006, but no new ones.
steps.highlight: Protection stops others using famous names

steps.prompt: What does PDO require that PGI does not?
options: All grapes from the defined area
steps.explanation: PDO requires all grapes from the area and stricter rules. PGI requires at least 85%.

steps.title: What you learned
points: A GI is a legally protected place name
Protection stops famous names being copied
